snapshot.capital_scaled: ₹15–40 lakh for 10+ products, own brand store and paid marketing
snapshot.margin_production: Contract manufacturing usually costs 15–25% of MRP; marketplaces leave you 35–45%
snapshot.distribution_note: Instagram and marketplaces are crowded; repeat buyers decide who survives

tailwinds: Quick-commerce apps now list small beauty and fragrance brands within weeks, and buyers in tier-2 cities order from them.
Contract manufacturers in Baddi, Delhi NCR, Ahmedabad and Bengaluru take first orders of 500–1,000 units, so you don't need a factory to launch.
Buyers actively look for Indian ingredients and origin stories: attars, Ayurvedic oils, saffron, rice water, sandalwood.
ONDC buyer apps let small sellers reach customers with lower commissions than the big marketplaces.
headwinds: Meta and Google ad costs keep rising; ₹400–1,200 to win a first order is common for new brands.
Large brands copy a trending ingredient within one or two quarters and outspend you on shelf space.
Cosmetic licensing, labelling and claims rules are stricter than most first-time founders expect.
Glass bottles and liquids mean breakage, leakage and returns on every courier route.
angle_2026: Three years ago a new personal-care brand could grow on Instagram ads alone. In 2026 the brands that last start narrow: one hero product, one clear community (men's grooming, curly hair, a regional ingredient) and a second sales channel such as salons, gyms, quick commerce or pop-ups before they scale ads.
cost_basis: Estimated for a small launch with a licensed contract manufacturer, 2–3 products and one city of focus, 2026 prices.

setup_costs.covers: 500–1,000 units per product from a licensed contract manufacturer, including formulation tweaks
Bottles or jars, labels, outer cartons and shipping inserts
Stability and patch tests, legal-metrology label review, trademark filing
Store setup, payment gateway, product listings on 1–2 marketplaces
Product shots, short videos, ingredient story

unit_economics.example: For a product priced at ₹499 MRP:
rows: Marketing per order in the first year
5–15% early on; 20–25% once repeat buyers are over a third of orders
unit_economics.note: The gross margin looks generous on paper. Marketing and marketplace fees are where it disappears, which is why repeat purchase matters more than any other number.

investor_probes: What share of customers buy again within 60 days?
How much does it cost to acquire a customer, compared with the average order value?
Why would a buyer choose you over a large brand's version of the same ingredient?
What happens if your only contract manufacturer raises prices or stops production?
Can every claim on the label be backed by a test?
bootstrap_takeaway: Launch with one product people reorder every month. Sell the first 500 units through WhatsApp, salons, gyms and friends-of-friends, and only start paid ads once more than a quarter of buyers come back within 30 days.
sourcing_edge: If your story is built on a regional ingredient, buy it where it is made. Direct purchase from the cluster usually cuts raw-material cost by 20–40% and gives you a provenance story (and sometimes a GI tag) that a big brand can't copy.
licences: Cosmetic manufacturing licence from your State Licensing Authority, or a licensed contract manufacturer named on your label
Legal Metrology declarations on every retail pack (MRP, net quantity, manufacturer and customer-care details)
GST registration (marketplaces ask for it at onboarding)
Trademark application for your brand name

hard_truths.title: The CAC trap
hard_truths.text: Many new brands pay ₹500–1,000 in ads to win a first order worth under ₹500. That only works if the customer comes back two or three times. If your 60-day repeat rate is under 20%, more ad spend makes the loss bigger, not smaller.

hard_truths.title: Marketplace margin squeeze
hard_truths.text: Commissions, fixed fees, shipping charges and the discounts marketplaces push during sales can take 35–45% of MRP. Price your products for that reality from day one instead of assuming your website margin.

hard_truths.title: Shelf life and dead stock
hard_truths.text: Most cosmetics carry an 18–36 month shelf life, and marketplaces reject stock close to expiry. Slow products tie up cash and then have to be written off or sold at a steep discount.

hard_truths.title: The scale bottleneck
hard_truths.text: Somewhere around 2,000–3,000 orders a month, manufacturer minimum orders across 8–10 products can lock ₹10–15 lakh into stock. That's the point where many founders run out of cash even though sales are growing.

plan_goal: The aim is ₹1 lakh in sales and a real repeat-purchase number before you commit to bigger batches.

plan.title: Validate and source
steps: Shortlist 3 licensed contract manufacturers and ask each for samples of your hero product.
Test 3–5 variants (fragrance, texture, pack size) with 30 people from your target buyers.
Price the product against 5 competitors, including one big brand.

plan.title: Compliance and pilot batch
steps: Get Udyam and GST registration and file your trademark.
Produce a pilot batch of 500 units with full, compliant labels.
Set up a simple website with UPI and cash-on-delivery.

plan.title: Sell directly
steps: Sell through WhatsApp groups, salons, gyms and a weekend pop-up before paying for ads.
Send 50 samples to micro-creators whose followers match your buyer.
Ask every buyer for a review and a photo.

plan.title: Review the numbers
steps: Measure repeat purchase, returns and cost per order across each channel.
Keep the channels that paid back; drop the rest.
Only then order the next batch and list on a marketplace.
